entries.principle_source: High-Level Expert Group on AI, Ethics Guidelines for Trustworthy AI (2019), Chapter II, Section 1.2
entries.provision: Article 5(1)(d) (benchmark — EU regulation does not bind this local prototype)
entries.why_here: Although Part 1 used clean synthetic profiles with 0/400 unparseable replies, rejecting out-of-range fields (such as impossible GPA or exam scores) before calling the model prevents corrupted inputs from receiving arbitrary scores.

entries.principle_source: UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence (2021), Section III.2, Paragraphs 29-31
entries.instrument: Law of the Republic of Kazakhstan No. 94-V 'On Personal Data and Their Protection', 21 May 2013
entries.provision: Article 12, Clause 2 (data sufficiency and purpose correspondence; read alongside Constitution of RK Article 14, Clause 2)
entries.why_here: Part 1 found 4/40 (10.0%) flips on gender-coded names, 2/40 (5.0%) flips on name language against a 0/40 floor, and a +2.5-point score gap (p = 0.002) favoring flagship universities, so hiding name and university removes non-merit cues from the prompt.

entries.principle: Right to Privacy, and Data Protection
entries.principle_source: UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence (2021), Section III.2, Paragraphs 32-34
entries.instrument: Law of the Republic of Kazakhstan No. 94-V 'On Personal Data and Their Protection', 21 May 2013
entries.why_here: Because Part 1 showed the bare agent unconditionally scores every profile passed to it without checking legal prerequisites, blocking prohibited purposes, minors under 18, missing consent, and prompt-injection strings stops unlawful or manipulated processing before inference.

entries.principle_source: OECD Recommendation of the Council on Artificial Intelligence (OECD/LEGAL/0449, 2019), Section 1.3 and Section 1.5
entries.provision: Article 12(1)-(2) (benchmark — EU regulation used as a technical standard alongside Law of RK No. 94-V, Article 22, Clause 1)
entries.why_here: Part 1 showed that individual prompts can shift scores even on null pairs (mean |diff| 2.00 for null_name and 2.12 for null_university) and the bare pipeline hides failures, so recording field names, input hashes, raw replies, and fired controls makes every verdict auditable.

entries.principle_source: UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence (2021), Section III.2, Paragraphs 35-36
entries.provision: Article 22(3) (benchmark — right to human intervention in automated decisions, alongside EU AI Act Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, Article 14)
entries.why_here: Part 1 revealed that shortlist and reject decisions overlap at score 45 (34/400 baseline profiles) and that n = 40 pairs cannot rule out effects below 15.0%, so routing score-45 ties, unparseable outputs, and sensitive-field rationales to a human prevents sole reliance on borderline automation.
